text.p: Long Island Lighting Co shareholders emerged on Monday as early winners in the $3 billion merger of LILCO and Brooklyn Union Gas Co, while Lilco's long-suffering ratepayers still need a state bailout to trim their sky-high electric bills.

But the overall success of the deal depends on New York's often contentious politics, analysts and traders said. They noted that the Long Island Power Authority still must rescue Lilco from debt incurred by construction of the $5 billion Shoreham nuclear power plant which never opened.

The agreement calls for Lilco shareholders to receive $25 per share, a price not seen since four years ago, in the fall of 1994. In New York Stock Exchange trade Monday, Lilco shares climbed 2-5/8 to 22 -- the highest level since early May 1995.
Brooklyn Union stock slipped 3/4 to 30 on Monday. Analysts said Brooklyn Union shareholders will benefit primarily from new opportunities to distribute natural gas on Long Island.
"The companies have said that if the Long Island Power Authority does not come up with billions, they will be faced with a very tough situation," said an analyst who asked not to be named.

"But the power authority, I expect, will make a move. In the merger, they are assuming the LIPA is going to come and take Shoreham off their hands. Brooklyn is picking up the bad operations of Lilco and there is an assumption that the state will get involved," he said.

Because of Shoreham, Lilco electric customers pay an average $0.1537 per kilowatt hour, the highest rate in the country, followed by Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc's $0.1354 per killowatt hour, the analyst said.
Even with the predicted 10 percent rate reduction from the merger, Lilco's rate will be third-highest in the nation and almost double the national average of $.0717 per killowatt hour.
Traders commenting on the deal said the political uncertainties will for the moment keep them from buying into the transaction.

"I am not going to go near it for a long time. The ratepayers are fuming, asking why the (Lilco) shareholders are being rewarded. It is going to a long, drawn out process that is going to hit a lot of political bumps," a trader said.
A second trader added," This deal is politics, politics, politcs. It is going to take a long, long time, and there are going to be a lot of political issues."
The transaction remains subject to shareholder and regulatory approval, and the companies said they expect it to close in 12 to 18 month.

In a reasearch note, PainWebber's natural gas equity research team stated, "The possibility exists that LIPA could come to an agreement with Lilco and Brooklyn Union to purchase Lilco's regulatory assets (Shoreham) and perhaps the electrical transmission and distribution assets of Lilco. If this were to occur the ratio for Lilco shareholders would adjust to 0.888 share of the (merged) company (from the current 0.803) for each share owned and the deal would probably be accounted for on a purchase basis (versus the current tax-free, pooling-of-interest accounting.)"
